chapters.title: Chapter I. How Candid was brought up in a magnificent castle, and how he was expelled from thence.
paragraphs: A young man lived in the Westphalian castle of Baron Thunder-ten-tronckh. Nature had given him an exceptionally gentle character, and you could read his thoughts in his face. He had good sense, together with an open, uncomplicated manner; that, I imagine, explains why he was called Candid. The older household servants suspected that his mother was the baron’s sister and his father a decent, kindly gentleman from nearby. The young lady had declined to marry this gentleman: he could show only seventy-one quarterings on his coat of arms, since the evidence for the others had been destroyed by the passage of time.

Among the lords of Westphalia the baron was particularly powerful: his castle possessed windows as well as a gate, and tapestries covered the walls of its great hall. When he hunted he took his mastiffs and spaniels in place of hunting hounds, with his stablemen serving as huntsmen. The local curate served as his grand almoner. Everyone addressed him as My Lord, and whenever he chose to tell a story, everyone could be relied on to laugh.

The baron’s wife weighed roughly three hundred and a half, which in itself earned her considerable reverence. Still greater respect was inspired by the dignity with which she received her guests. Her daughter, Cunegund, was seventeen: rosy, good-looking, pleasantly plump, and attractive. The young baron appeared to take after his father in every worthy respect. Their tutor, Pangloss, supplied the household with its oracular wisdom. Little Candid absorbed his lessons with the unassuming trust appropriate both to his years and to his natural disposition.

Pangloss held a professorship in metaphysico-theologo-cosmolo-nigology. His demonstrations were admirable: everything that happened had a cause; this world was the finest world that could possibly be; its most magnificent castle belonged to the baron; and no baroness could conceivably surpass the baron’s wife. He could prove every one of these propositions.

You can prove, he said, that things could not be arranged in any other way. Everything was created with a purpose, so that purpose must necessarily be the best one. Consider the nose: it was shaped to carry spectacles, which explains our wearing them. Legs were plainly designed to take stockings, which explains our stockings. Stone was made for cutting and building castles; accordingly, my lord possesses a magnificent castle, since the foremost baron in the province deserves the finest accommodation. Pigs were intended for eating, which explains our eating pork throughout the year. People who maintain that everything is right therefore use an inaccurate expression: they ought to say that everything is as good as it can be.

Candid paid close attention and accepted it all without question, since he considered Miss Cunegund extraordinarily beautiful, although he never dared say so to her. He reckoned that the greatest happiness was to be Baron Thunder-ten-tronckh; being Miss Cunegund came second, seeing her each day third. After those came the pleasure of listening to Master Pangloss expound his teaching. Pangloss was the province’s foremost philosopher and must therefore be the foremost philosopher anywhere on earth.

During a walk one day in the small wood nearby, known as the park, Cunegund peered through the bushes and caught sight of Doctor Pangloss instructing her mother’s chambermaid in experimental philosophy. This was a small, dark girl, very pretty and very willing to learn. Miss Cunegund had a strong inclination towards scientific study, so she watched with the closest attention as the experiments were repeated in front of her. The force of the doctor’s reasoning about cause and effect became perfectly clear to her. She turned homewards deeply stirred, lost in thought, and hungry for knowledge, imagining that she could provide young Candid with a sufficient reason, and he could provide one for her.

She encountered the young man on her way home and blushed; he blushed too. Her voice shook as she wished him good morning, and he answered without any idea of what he was saying. After dinner the following day, Cunegund and Candid slipped behind the screen. She let her handkerchief fall, and he picked it up. Quite innocently she took his hand; with equal innocence, he kissed hers, displaying a most remarkable eagerness, feeling, and grace. They kissed; their eyes shone; their knees shook; their hands began to wander . . . . . Passing just then, Baron Thunder-ten-tronckh witnessed this instance of cause and effect, kicked Candid in the backside, and sent him out of the house. Miss Cunegund lost consciousness. As soon as she recovered, the baroness slapped her about the ears. In this way dismay overtook the entire castle, the most magnificent and delightful castle that could possibly be.
